index.html.title: IKE Doc Maven Plugin
index.html.body:
IKE Doc Maven Plugin The ike-doc-maven-plugin provides the idoc:* goal prefix — AsciiDoc rendering, multi-renderer PDF wrappers (Prince, Apache FOP, RenderX XEP, Antenna House, WeasyPrint), DocBook XSL patching, breadcrumb injection for site navigation, renderer log scanning, and doc-diff review packets (idoc:diff). Coordinate Value Group ID network.ike.docs Artifact ID ike-doc-maven-plugin Goal prefix idoc: Packaging maven-plugin Java version 25 For workspace-spanning goals (ws:* prefix), see the ws plugin[1] in ike-platform. For single-repo release orchestration (ike:*), see the ike plugin[2] in ike-tooling. The three plugins are deliberately separate — idoc:* is doc rendering, ike:* is single-repo release, ws:* fans out across a workspace’s checked-out subprojects. For people who work through Claude rather than a terminal, The Topic Registry: A Plain-Language Guide[3] walks through idoc:topic-registry with a tutorial and every action it offers. Plugin shape This is a regular Maven plugin — no <extensions>true</extensions>, no custom <packaging> type registered via META-INF/plexus/components.xml, no participation in the build extension realm. Goals look up at execution time, the plugin’s <version> interpolates from ${ike-docs.version} like any other managed plugin, and consumers inherit the version through ordinary <pluginManagement> indirection. This was not always the case. Earlier revisions registered the <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> custom type here, which forced this plugin to be loaded as a build extension and consequently forced its <version> to be a literal string everywhere it was declared. That constraint was retired alongside the migration to a classifier-canonical doc shape (see Design rationale below). What this means for plugin consumers: nothing changes about how you invoke idoc:* goals. What changed is that the plugin no longer forces literal-version pins in your POM, and no longer contributes <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> to your reactor. Doc modules now use <packaging>pom</packaging> (or <packaging>jar</packaging> for hybrid Java-plus-docs modules) plus an adoc classifier attachment; activation is path-conditional on src/docs/asciidoc/ existence in ike-parent’s `doc-pipeline profile. Goals at a glance Goal Purpose idoc:asciidoc Render AsciiDoc sources via AsciidoctorJ — the heart of the doc pipeline. Handles IKE-specific renderer profiles (Prawn / Prince / AH / WeasyPrint / XEP / FOP / DocBook / single-page HTML). idoc:render-pdf Wrapper around the five external PDF renderers (Prince, AH, FOP, WeasyPrint, XEP). Selects the active renderer per -Dike.pdf.<name>=true toggles set by the doc-pipeline profile. idoc:diff Generate and render a review packet: every changed AsciiDoc topic between two refs (or a ref and the working tree), marked inline with insertion/deletion roles. See Review packets below. idoc:topic-registry Read the :topic-*: header of every AsciiDoc file under the module’s source root and write target/topic-registry.yaml: the topic registry, generated from the headers in `IKE-TOPIC-REGISTRY.md’s shape instead of kept by hand. See Topic registry below. idoc:adocstudio Generate Adoc Studio sidecar projects for assembly modules. idoc:patch-docbook Patch the stock DocBook XSL 1.79.2 stylesheets to suppress two known Saxon warnings. Applied during the docbook-xsl artifact build. idoc:fix-svg Remove bare <rect/> elements that Mermaid emits as artifacts in generated HTML — they cause rendering glitches in some browsers. idoc:inject-breadcrumb Inject navigation breadcrumbs and theme overrides into JaCoCo HTML reports so they fit visually with the rest of the Maven site. idoc:copy-default-pdf Promote one renderer’s PDF as the default. With multiple renderers producing output in pdf-prince/, pdf-fop/, etc., this picks the first available and copies it to a single canonical pdf/ location. idoc:prepare-renderer-output Create the per-renderer output directories (pdf-prince/, pdf-fop/, etc.) before the renderers run. idoc:scan-logs Scan renderer log files (renderer-*.log) for error patterns and print a summary. Used after multi-renderer runs to flag failures fast. idoc:package-doc Zip src/docs/asciidoc/ and assign as primary artifact. Originally bound to the <package> phase of the retired ike-doc lifecycle; superseded by maven-assembly-plugin’s `adoc classifier execution in ike-parent’s `doc-pipeline profile. Retained at present pending a final decision in the open question on ike-issues#321[4]; may be removed in a follow-up. Review packets (idoc:diff) Reviewing documentation changes offers two bad currencies: git diff is source-true but contextless; rendered books carry context but no deltas. idoc:diff closes the gap — a generated, renderable review packet in which every changed topic appears as its own chapter with word-level [.diff-ins]/[.diff-del] markup in place, deletions struck through, insertions highlighted, and non-prose changes (attributes, index terms, table and diagram interiors) reported in a per-topic change-summary note. Changed diagrams render alongside their source delta and previous rendering. mvn idoc:diff                                    # HEAD vs working tree
mvn idoc:diff -Dike.diff.from=v1.2.3             # tag vs working tree
mvn idoc:diff -Dike.diff.from=A -Dike.diff.to=B  # any two commits
mvn idoc:diff -Dike.diff.topics=arch-overview    # share-scoped excerpt The goal works at the Maven subproject level: a topics-library module (one whose source root holds topics/) yields the corpus packet (with an entry-keyed topic-registry delta); an assembly module yields the projection of the diff onto the topics its include:: lines name; an aggregator invocation produces a packet for every subproject able to generate one. The registry on each side is generated from the files on that side, as idoc:topic-registry would; no hand-kept registry file is read. Outputs land in target/doc-diff/ as packet sources, HTML, and a Prawn PDF — the goal is self-contained, so a bare invocation on a fresh checkout produces a styled packet (branded typography when the pipeline fonts are unpacked; a bundled fallback theme otherwise). Files a marked topic pulls in by relative include:: — diagram sources, shared snippets — are staged beside it, so an include that resolves from the source tree resolves from the packet too. Changes are first-class, named entities: author a changes.yaml beside the module pom (or at the repository root) with an id, title, one-line description, issue refs, and touched files per change — or, for commit-to-commit comparisons, let the goal derive entities by grouping the range’s commits on their Refs:/Fixes: trailers. The entities project into a Record of Changes, a Change Glossary, and an index-driven Change Index. Each change boundary also carries a STAMP endnote — Status (Active/Inactive), Time, Author, Module (topic domain), Path (branch) — collapsed per paragraph and tabulated in a Stamp Register. Design note: dev-doc-diff-pipeline in ike-lab-documents/topics/; epic ike-issues#648[5]. Topic registry (idoc:topic-registry) idoc:topic-registry is the topic registry’s build-time revision: the registry keeps the shape IKE-TOPIC-REGISTRY.md gives it and is now generated from the files on every run instead of typed by hand. The goal reads the :topic-*: attribute block, the anchor and the level-1 heading of every .adoc file under the module’s src/docs/asciidoc — plain line parsing, no AsciidoctorJ — and writes target/topic-registry.yaml in the shape IKE-TOPIC-REGISTRY.md gives the registry: registry-version, generated, topic-count, then domains, one per id prefix, each with its topics in id order (id, file, title, type, keywords, status, char-count, related, summary, and what the header adds: provenance, anchor, header, …). After the domains come assemblies (files with include:: lines, with their counts), other-files, and a findings list. The file that was kept by hand at src/docs/asciidoc/topic-registry.yaml is no longer maintained; neither this goal nor idoc:diff reads it, so it can be deleted once its values are moved into topic headers. What a header cannot say is not generated: domain titles and descriptions, assembly sections and topic-refs, and dependencies unless a header declares them. The same structure is printed to the build log as a directory tree. Symbolic links are never followed (a linked .adoc is a finding), files are parsed in parallel, and the YAML is written directly, so a 20,000-file module rebuilds in well under a second. mvn idoc:topic-registry                                          # the module's src/docs/asciidoc
mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.roots=a,b           # other roots, comma-separated
mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.output=/tmp/r.yaml  # write elsewhere
mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.add=topics/x/new.adoc   # add an ingested file, no rescan With -Dike.topic-registry.add= (comma-separated files, relative to the module or absolute) the named files are parsed alone and merged into the existing registry: placed in their domain in id order, counted, and checked for a duplicate id against the ids the registry already holds. An entry for the same file is replaced, so re-ingesting a document is safe. Files that were deleted are not noticed this way; a run without add re-derives everything, and runs when no generated registry exists yet. Header findings — a missing required attribute, an anchor that does not match the id, an unknown type or status, the same id in two files — are reported in the registry and the log and do not fail the build. A module without src/docs/asciidoc is skipped with one line, so the goal can run from a reactor root. -Dike.skip.topic-registry=true skips it. The goal’s default phase is validate, so a POM that declares an execution of it gets a fresh registry on every build, mvn clean install included, and findings still do not fail that build: <plugin>
  <groupId>network.ike.docs</groupId>
  <artifactId>ike-doc-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>topic-registry</id>
      <goals><goal>topic-registry</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin> Design rationale This plugin’s shape — regular plugin, no extensions, no custom packaging — is the result of a deliberate architectural decision documented in ike-issues#321[4] and the dev-classifier-canonical-doc-shape topic in ike-lab-documents/topics/. Brief summary, since the issue will eventually close and this page is what surviving teams will land on: Why no extensions A plugin with <extensions>true</extensions> is loaded into the build extension realm at project-load time — during Maven’s “Scanning for projects” phase, before the Model Builder runs property interpolation. This means the plugin’s <version> in the POM cannot be a ${property}; it must be a literal string. For a single-repo reactor with one plugin, the constraint is manageable. For our cross-repo cascade (ike-tooling → ike-docs → ike-platform → consumers), it became toxic: every consumer POM had to carry the literal version of every extension plugin from upstream, the literal had to be kept in sync manually across repos, and routine version-property tooling (ws:align-publish, versions:set-property) was structurally unable to maintain it. The pain surfaced as ike-issues#236[6] — pre-flight release checks repeatedly catching stale literals after upstream releases that the alignment tooling could not see. Why no <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> The historical reason for <extensions>true</extensions> here was to register a custom <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> type for documentation modules — a packaging that produces a .zip of AsciiDoc sources as the primary artifact, with a lean lifecycle that skips compile/test phases. Inspection revealed two structural problems with that frame: The custom packaging produced a primary artifact nobody used. Across 43 <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> modules in ike-lab-documents, zero dependencies referenced <type>ike-doc</type>. Consumers exclusively used a parallel <classifier>asciidoc</classifier><type>zip</type> attachment (built by maven-assembly-plugin from the same source directory). Same content, two coordinates, redundant. Custom packaging cannot serve hybrid modules. <packaging> is single-valued: a Java module that ships reference docs cannot be both jar and ike-doc. Hybrid modules are the norm in any non-trivial project. Every comparable docs-as-code project in the JVM ecosystem (Hibernate, Eclipse Collections, Vert.x, Quarkus, OptaPlanner, Apache projects) handles this via classifier attachments for exactly this reason. No project in the surveyed set invents a custom packaging type for documentation. The architectural decision was therefore to retire <packaging>ike-doc</packaging> in favor of a classifier- canonical shape: <classifier>adoc</classifier><type>zip</type> attached to either a <packaging>pom</packaging> (doc-only) or <packaging>jar</packaging> (hybrid) primary. Activation is path-conditional on src/docs/asciidoc/ existence in ike-parent’s `doc-pipeline profile — not packaging type — so hybrid modules become first-class without per-module ceremony. The artifact-uniformity argument for staying Maven-canonical A natural objection: most large JVM projects (Spring, many Apache projects, Quarkus) publish docs as static sites to gh-pages or CDN-hosted destinations rather than as Maven artifacts. Why not follow that pattern? Examined point-by-point, those rationales do not transfer. Most of the apparent reasons (continuous publication, search-driven discovery, contributor friction, CDN economics) have Maven-snapshot-plus-post-deploy-rsync solutions and so do not argue against staying inside the Maven artifact ecosystem. What genuinely remains as a non-Maven argument — Antora as a turnkey product — does not apply here, because we have already built the equivalent rendering pipeline (`ike-parent’s render profiles, Prince/FOP/XEP chains, knowledge.design rsync deploy, the asciidoctor toolchain). Spring would have to throw away their pipeline to gain Antora’s turnkey-ness; we have ours, so the comparison does not apply. For our constraints — small team, cross-repo doc dependencies via topic libraries, an already-built rendering pipeline, and a standing commitment to artifact uniformity — staying inside the Maven artifact ecosystem is the rigorous choice. We hold every shipped artifact, code or documentation, to the same engineering standard: signed (Bouncy Castle GPG, parallel-safe), versioned, deployed to Nexus, mirrorable, and reproducibly buildable years later. We do not want one class of output operating under different rules than another. The single-pipeline discipline is the standard we are protecting. The classifier-canonical shape is fully Maven-canonical — every artifact deploys to Nexus, signed and versioned, just like every other output of the project. The choice between custom packaging and classifier is not a Maven-vs-non-Maven choice; both stay inside the Maven ecosystem. Custom packaging was buying an aesthetic type-system marker; classifier-canonical buys a single mechanism that handles doc-only and hybrid uniformly. Tracking ike-issues#321[4] — primary tracking issue (umbrella); subsumes #220, #236, #320. ike-issues#216[7] — repo split that established the cross-repo boundary the extension realm was working around. Design note: dev-classifier-canonical-doc-shape in ike-lab-documents/topics/ (full Socratic discovery captured for posterity). See also ike:* plugin in ike-tooling[2] — single-repo release orchestration. ws:* plugin in ike-platform[1] — workspace-spanning goals. ike-docs reactor home[8]. Source on GitHub[9]. Issue tracker[10].

topic-registry-guide.html.title: The Topic Registry: A Plain-Language Guide
topic-registry-guide.html.body:
The Topic Registry: A Plain-Language Guide The topic registry is the catalog of a project’s documents. With this update it is built automatically: one command reads every document file, lists what is there, grouped by subject area, and points out labeling problems, without changing anything. This guide is for people who work through Claude rather than a terminal. For the technical reference, see the plugin page[1]. 1. What is the topic registry Who this is for Anyone who writes, reviews or looks after documents in an IKE project and works through Claude rather than a terminal: authors, reviewers, regulatory and quality staff, and project leads. No knowledge of Maven, Git or AsciiDoc is assumed. Purpose To give you a trustworthy, current picture of a project’s documents (what exists, where it is stored, which subject area it belongs to and whether each one is labeled correctly) in a few seconds, so that gaps are caught before a review or a submission rather than during one. The registry is a fresh catalog of every document in a project, built by reading the label block at the top of each file. Think of a librarian walking the shelves and writing down each book’s title, subject and condition, instead of trusting an old card catalog that someone typed by hand. Use it when you want to know: What documents exist in this project, in which folders and under which subject areas? Is every document labeled properly (name, type, status, keywords)? What has been added since the catalog was last built? The technical name is idoc:topic-registry. It is a command in the IKE documentation toolkit and works on any IKE documentation project, large or small. A test on a 290-document project finished in under a tenth of a second. Before this update the registry was typed by hand, as a topic-registry.yaml file kept next to the documents. That file is no longer maintained; the registry the build writes is the current record. You do not need to type commands. Ask Claude in plain words, as shown under each action below. The exact command is listed for reference. 2. Tutorial: your first registry This walk-through takes about ten minutes. You will build the registry, read it, fix a problem it reports, and add a new document to it. The file names are made up for illustration; yours will differ. 2.1. Step 1: Build the registry First, open the project in Claude. "The project" is the folder on your computer that holds the documents. Opening it tells Claude which folder to work in. In the Claude desktop app (Mac or Windows) Open the Claude app and switch to the Code tab. Choose the project folder when Claude asks where to work. Pick the top folder of the project, the one that contains a file named pom.xml, not the documents folder inside it. Start a new session. The folder name shown in the session confirms you are in the right place. In a web browser Go to https://claude.ai/code[2] and sign in. Pick the project’s repository from the list. This needs the project to be on GitHub and your GitHub account to be connected; Claude walks you through connecting it the first time. If the project is not on your computer yet, ask the person who maintains it for the GitHub address, then tell Claude in the desktop app: "Download the project at <address> and open it." To check that you are in the right place, ask: "Which folder are you working in, and does it have a pom.xml?" Once the project is open, say: Build the topic registry for this project. Claude runs the command and shows you the result. Nothing in your project changes. 2.2. Step 2: Read the list The result is a folder-by-folder list, followed by one summary line: src/docs/asciidoc
  topics/
    cleaning-steps.adoc         ops-cleaning-steps     procedure  -
    device-description.adoc     dev-device-description concept    draft
  submission.adoc               assembly, 2 includes
registry: topics/cleaning-steps.adoc: missing required attribute :topic-status:
2 topics, 1 other file, 1 finding; topic registry written to target/topic-registry.yaml (41 ms) Read it like this: Each labeled document shows four things: its file name, its name (id), its type and its status. A dash means that label is missing. Here cleaning-steps.adoc has no status. The first part of a name, before the first hyphen, is its subject area: ops for ops-cleaning-steps, dev for dev-device-description. The saved file groups documents by it. submission.adoc is a binder: a file that pulls two other documents together. The line starting with registry: is a finding. It names the file and says what is wrong. The last line counts everything and says where the registry file was saved. 2.3. Step 3: Fix the finding The finding says cleaning-steps.adoc is missing its status label. You can fix it yourself by adding this line to the label block at the top of the file: :topic-status: draft Or let Claude do it: Fix what the topic registry reported. The registry itself never edits a document. Any change is made by you or by Claude, where you can review it. 2.4. Step 4: Run it again Say: Build the topic registry again. The registry is rebuilt from scratch. The dash is replaced by draft, and the summary line now ends in 0 findings. That is the whole routine: run, read, fix, run again. 2.5. Step 5: Add a new document Suppose a new document, storage-conditions.adoc, has just been added to the topics folder. You do not have to re-read the whole collection. Say: Add topics/storage-conditions.adoc to the topic registry. The result is short: registry: topic ops-storage-conditions at topics/storage-conditions.adoc
added 1 file to target/topic-registry.yaml without rescanning (12 ms) The new document is now in the registry, placed in its subject area and checked like every other document. 2.6. Step 6: Look something up The saved registry is what Claude reads when you ask about the project’s documents. Say, for example: Which documents in the topic registry cover storage conditions, and what status are they in? If the project still has the hand-typed registry file next to the documents from before the update, you can also ask: Compare the built registry with the hand-typed file and list the differences. The built registry is the current record. You have now used every part of the registry you are likely to need. The rest of this guide is reference. 3. Actions you can take There are six actions. Action 1 is the one you will use almost every time. The others adjust it. # Action Ask Claude 1 Build the registry "Build the topic registry for this project." 2 Add new documents without re-reading everything "Add the file X to the topic registry." 3 Look in different folders "Build the topic registry from the folders X and Y." 4 Save the registry somewhere else "Build the topic registry and save it to Z." 5 Allow a very large collection "Build the topic registry and raise the file limit to 10,000." 6 Turn the registry off "Skip the topic registry for this run." 3.1. Action 1: Build the registry What it does Reads every document file in the project’s standard documents folder and produces the catalog. What you get A folder-by-folder list on screen, a saved registry file, and a one-line summary such as "3 topics, 1 other file, 0 findings". Good to know If the project has no documents folder, the registry says so in one line and moves on. That is normal, not an error. It lets one request cover a whole group of projects at once. A project can also be set up so that the registry is rebuilt on every build; the plugin page shows how. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry 3.2. Action 2: Add new documents without re-reading everything What it does Reads only the files you name and merges them into the registry that already exists. List several files separated by commas. When to use it One or a few documents were just added or changed, and the collection is large enough that you do not want to re-read all of it. Good to know Adding the same file twice is safe; the newer entry replaces the older one. The new document’s name is checked against the registry, so a duplicate name is still caught. If no registry exists yet, a full build (Action 1) runs instead. Deleted documents are not noticed this way. After deleting or moving documents, use Action 1. Each file must be a document file inside one of the folders the registry covers. Otherwise the run stops and says which file to check. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.add=src/docs/asciidoc/topics/storage-conditions.adoc 3.3. Action 3: Look in different folders What it does Points the registry at one or more folders you name, instead of the standard documents folder. List several folders separated by commas. When to use it Your documents live somewhere unusual, or you only care about one part of the collection. Good to know If a folder you name does not exist, the run stops and tells you which folder to check. This protects you from a typo silently producing an empty catalog. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.roots=folderA,folderB 3.4. Action 4: Save the registry somewhere else What it does Writes the registry file to a location you choose. Normally it goes into the project’s temporary build folder as target/topic-registry.yaml. When to use it You want to keep a copy to share, or to compare two runs side by side. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.output=/path/to/registry.yaml 3.5. Action 5: Allow a very large collection What it does Raises the safety limit on how many document files one folder may hold. The limit is 5,000 files. When to use it Only when a run stops with the message "More than 5000 .adoc files". The limit exists to catch the registry being pointed at the wrong, enormous folder by mistake. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.topic-registry.maxFiles=10000 3.6. Action 6: Turn the registry off What it does Skips the registry for one run. Nothing is read and nothing is written. When to use it The registry is part of a larger automated job and you do not need it this time. Exact command mvn idoc:topic-registry -Dike.skip.topic-registry=true Actions 3, 4 and 5 can be combined in a single request. 4. What you get back Every full run gives you three things: a list on screen, a saved file, and a summary line. The on-screen list Folders, then each file inside. A labeled document shows its name, type and status. Any other file shows whether it is a binder that pulls other documents together, or a plain file. Step 2 of the tutorial shows an example. The registry file A saved, structured catalog with more detail, in the standard IKE registry layout: labeled documents grouped by subject area, then binders, then plain files, then findings. This is the file Claude reads when you ask what the project contains. The summary line Counts of labeled documents, other files and problems found, plus where the file was saved and how long the run took. For each labeled document For every other file Name (id), file location and title File location and title Type, status and origin Whether it is a binder (assembly) or a plain file Keywords, summary and related documents How many documents it pulls in Length in characters Its document settings Whether the label block is complete, or what is missing The registry file is rebuilt from scratch on every full run. Do not edit it and do not store it with the project’s documents. If you want to keep one, use Action 4. 5. Problems it points out The registry reports labeling problems, called findings, but never stops the run because of them. Each finding names the file it concerns. Findings appear as warnings on screen and in a list at the end of the registry file. The message says What it means How to fix it missing required attribute The label block lacks one of the four required labels: name (id), type, status or keywords. Add the missing label at the top of the file. unknown type The type is not one of: concept, task, procedure, reference, dialog. Change it to one of the five. unknown status The status is not one of: draft, proposed, review, published, deprecated. Change it to one of the five. no anchor before the heading The bookmark that lets other documents link to this one is missing. Add the bookmark line, matching the document’s name. anchor does not match The bookmark and the document’s name differ, so links may break. Make the two identical. no level-1 heading The document has no main title. Add a title line. duplicate id Two files claim the same name. The message names both. Rename one of them. symbolic link, skipped The file is a shortcut to another file. Shortcuts are never followed, so it was not read. Usually none needed. Replace the shortcut with a real file if it belongs here. Only labeled documents are checked. Binders and plain files are listed but never produce findings. 6. What it never does The registry only reads your documents and writes one file of its own. It is safe to run at any time, as often as you like. It never edits, moves, renames or deletes a document. It never touches the registry file that was typed by hand before the update. That file is no longer maintained; the built registry is the current record. It never fails a run because of a labeling problem. Problems are reported, not enforced. It never reads outside the folders it was given. Shortcuts that point elsewhere are skipped and reported. It ignores working folders that hold no real documents (target, .git, node_modules). A run stops early in only a few cases: a folder or file you named does not exist or is outside the registry’s folders (Actions 2 and 3), the file limit is exceeded (Action 5), or a file or folder cannot be read or written. Each message says what to check. 7. Words used in this guide Word Meaning Document file A text file ending in .adoc, the format IKE documents are written in (AsciiDoc). Label block The lines at the top of a document that state its name, type, status, keywords and other details. Technically, the :topic-*: header. Labeled document (topic) A document that has a label block with a name. Subject area (domain) The first part of a document’s name, before the first hyphen: ops in ops-cleaning-steps. The registry groups documents by it. Binder (assembly) A file that pulls other documents together into one larger document. Plain file A document file with no label block that pulls nothing in. Topic registry The automatically built catalog, target/topic-registry.yaml. Registry file before the update The hand-typed topic-registry.yaml kept next to the documents, no longer maintained now that the registry is built on every run. Finding A labeling problem the registry noticed.

built-with.html.title: Built With
built-with.html.body: Built With Open-source software that ike-doc-maven-plugin 124 depends on, links against, ships within, or invokes at runtime. Three layers of attribution ship with each release: Software Bill of Materials (CycloneDX, JSON)[1] — full transitive dependency graph with SPDX-normalized licenses and artifact hashes. Ingestible by Dependency-Track, Trivy, Snyk, GitHub’s dependency graph. Licenses (SPDX)[2] — human-readable SPDX-grouped view of declared dependencies, generated from bom.json (#335). This page — curated companion covering what mechanical reports can’t see (Maven Site skin, external services, fonts inside artifacts, frontend assets in rendered HTML). Curated narrative Components covered by the project-wide supplement at src/main/built-with/supplement.yaml. These are the components that don’t appear in bom.json because they aren’t Maven artifacts (external services, fonts inside classifier ZIPs, runtime binaries, frontend assets). AsciiDoc rendering toolchain Component License Role AsciidoctorJ[3] MIT The Java entry-point for the Asciidoctor renderer. ike-doc-maven-plugin invokes it via the official Maven plugin to convert .adoc source to HTML, DocBook, and XHTML. AsciidoctorJ PDF[4] MIT Direct PDF rendering of AsciiDoc. The prawn profile in ike-parent activates this renderer; output is post- processed for page-break and font handling. AsciidoctorJ Diagram[5] MIT Inline diagram rendering. Used together with the Kroki extension to support PlantUML, Graphviz, Mermaid, and similar formats inside AsciiDoc source. Asciidoctor Maven Plugin[6] MIT The Maven plugin wrapper that drives AsciidoctorJ from the build. Asciidoctor Parser Doxia Module[7] MIT Lets maven-site-plugin natively render src/site/asciidoc/*.adoc alongside the auto-generated reports. (Replaced an earlier pre-render step in #310.) JRuby[8] EPL-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only OR LGPL-2.1-only Embedded Ruby runtime that Asciidoctor itself runs on. Pulled in transitively by AsciidoctorJ. Koncept AsciiDoc Extension[9] MIT In-house extension (vendored in this reactor as koncept-asciidoc-extension) that adds Koncept macros to AsciiDoc source. Diagram rendering Component License Role Kroki (PlantUML, Graphviz, Mermaid, BlockDiag, etc. backends)[10] MIT External HTTP service that renders diagram blocks. The IKE Network runs a private Kroki instance at kroki.komet.sh; documents that contain diagram blocks call it at render time. Each backend has its own license — PlantUML (GPL-3.0), Graphviz (CPL-1.0), Mermaid (MIT), etc. Diagrams render server-side; the rendered SVG/PNG is embedded in the output. External PDF renderers (runtime, not bundled) Component License Role Prince XML[11] Commercial (out of SPDX scope); free for personal/non-commercial use High-quality CSS-Paged-Media renderer used by the pdf-prince profile. Antenna House Formatter[12] Commercial (out of SPDX scope) XSL-FO renderer used by the pdf-ah profile. WeasyPrint[13] BSD-3-Clause CSS-Paged-Media renderer (Python) used by the pdf-weasy profile. Apache FOP[14] Apache-2.0 XSL-FO renderer used by the pdf-fop profile. RenderX XEP[15] Commercial (out of SPDX scope); free personal license available XSL-FO renderer used by the pdf-xep profile. DocBook toolchain Component License Role DocBook XSL Stylesheets 1.0[16] MIT XSL transformation rules from DocBook → HTML/XSL-FO/etc. Wrapped by the ike-docs:docbook-xsl module which repackages a curated subset for IKE consumers. Saxon-HE[17] MPL-2.0 XSLT 2.0/3.0 processor used to apply DocBook XSL transformations. Fonts (embedded in rendered PDFs and bundled in classified artifacts) Component License Role Noto Serif, Noto Sans, Noto Sans Mono, Noto Math, Noto Sans Symbols[18] OFL-1.1 Default body, sans-serif, monospace, math, and symbol typefaces. Distributed via ike-docs:minimal-fonts as a classified artifact consumed by all PDF and printable HTML renderers. The full SIL Open Font License 1.1 text is included in the minimal-fonts artifact and reproduced in any rendered PDF that embeds these fonts. Frontend assets (bundled in rendered HTML) Component License Role Font Awesome (free tier — icons, fonts, JS)[19] CC-BY-4.0 AND OFL-1.1 AND MIT Icon set used in rendered HTML. Sentry skin pulls icons through the <i class="fa-…"> API. Different files under different licenses — icons CC-BY-4.0; fonts OFL-1.1; JS MIT. Prism[20] MIT Syntax highlighter for code blocks in rendered HTML. Embedded in the AsciiDoc pipeline output. Mechanical inventory Direct dependencies of this module, grouped by SPDX expression. Generated from bom.json at build time.
